questions.q: A client connects with no security settings at all. Which `security.protocol` does it use?

options.why: SSL must be configured; the default is PLAINTEXT.
SASL_SSL must be configured; the default is PLAINTEXT.

options.t: Whatever the broker's first listener uses, discovered automatically
options.why: The client's protocol is its own setting, defaulting to PLAINTEXT.

questions.explain: `security.protocol` defaults to `PLAINTEXT`; the other values are `SSL`, `SASL_PLAINTEXT` and `SASL_SSL`.

questions.q: A cluster's client listener uses SASL/SCRAM over TLS. Which TWO client settings are part of connecting to it?

options.why: That is SASL without TLS; SCRAM should only be used with TLS.
The default is GSSAPI (Kerberos), not SCRAM.
That turns off hostname verification, which the docs warn against.

questions.explain: SCRAM over TLS is `security.protocol=SASL_SSL` with `sasl.mechanism` set to a SCRAM mechanism (the default mechanism is GSSAPI), plus `sasl.jaas.config` with the credentials.

questions.q: Which client setting carries the SASL login module and credentials?

options.why: That names the mechanism, not the credentials.
That is for TLS client certificates.
client.id is a logical name for request logs.

questions.explain: `sasl.jaas.config` holds the JAAS login context: `loginModuleClass controlFlag (optionName=optionValue)*;`.

questions.q: Brokers require client certificates (mTLS, `ssl.client.auth=required`). What does the client need besides a trust store?

options.t: Nothing more; a trust store is enough for mTLS
options.why: A trust store only lets the client trust the brokers; mTLS needs the client's own certificate.
mTLS authenticates with certificates, not SASL.

options.t: A key store with its own certificate (ssl.keystore.location)

options.why: With mTLS the client is identified by its certificate, not as ANONYMOUS.

questions.explain: The trust store lets the client trust the brokers' certificates; for two-way (mutual) TLS the client also presents its own certificate from its key store, which is optional otherwise.

questions.q: A developer gets certificate errors connecting by IP address and proposes disabling `ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm`. What do the Kafka docs advise?

options.t: Disabling it is fine in production if the trust store is private
options.why: The docs warn against disabling hostname verification.
That's a broker setting, and the docs call 'requested' a false sense of security.

options.t: Switch to SASL_PLAINTEXT to avoid certificates
options.why: That removes encryption in transit.

options.t: Keep hostname verification on; fix the certificate

questions.explain: Hostname verification is on by default (`https`). The docs warn against disabling it and prefer the subject alternative name (SAN) field over the common name.

questions.q: Which statement about SASL/PLAIN is right?

options.t: It encrypts passwords, so it is safe on PLAINTEXT listeners
options.why: PLAIN sends credentials as they are; it should only be used with TLS.

options.t: It should only be used with TLS
It is the same as the PLAINTEXT security protocol
options.why: PLAINTEXT is a protocol with no security; SASL/PLAIN is a username/password mechanism.

options.t: It is Kafka's default SASL mechanism
options.why: The default is GSSAPI.

questions.explain: SASL/PLAIN and SCRAM should be used only with TLS (SASL_SSL); OAUTHBEARER should only be used with TLS in production.

questions.q: Using `kafka-acls`, a team grants a service `--producer` on topic `orders`. What does that grant?

options.why: It also grants DESCRIBE and CREATE.

options.t: READ and WRITE on the topic
options.why: READ is what --consumer grants.
It is scoped to the topic.

options.t: WRITE, DESCRIBE and CREATE on the topic

questions.explain: `kafka-acls --producer` grants WRITE, DESCRIBE and CREATE on the topic; `--consumer` grants READ and DESCRIBE on the topic and READ on the group.

questions.q: A consumer has an ACL allowing READ on topic `orders`, but its consumer group `billing` has no ACL. With the StandardAuthorizer and default settings, what happens when it subscribes in that group?

options.t: It is denied: it also needs READ on the group
It works: groups don't have ACLs
options.why: Groups are resources; --consumer grants READ on the group for this reason.

options.t: It works because topic READ implies group READ
options.why: Each resource needs its own allowing ACL.

options.t: It works because resources without ACLs are open to everyone
options.why: By default, a resource with no ACLs is accessible only to super users.

questions.explain: Principals without an allowing ACL are denied, and a resource with no ACLs is open only to super users (unless `allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true`). A consumer needs READ on the topic and READ on the group.

questions.q: A principal has an ALLOW ACL for WRITE on topic `orders` and a DENY ACL for WRITE on the prefix `ord`. Can it write to `orders`?

options.t: Yes; a literal ACL beats a prefixed one
options.why: Any matching DENY wins, regardless of ALLOW ACLs.

options.t: Yes; ALLOW ACLs are checked first
options.why: DENY is checked and wins if it matches.

options.t: No; a matching DENY wins over any ALLOW
It depends on which ACL was created last
options.why: Creation order doesn't matter.

questions.explain: If any DENY ACL matches, the operation is denied regardless of ALLOW ACLs (StandardAuthorizer).

questions.q: Which ACL operation does a principal need on a topic to change its configuration (for example `retention.ms`)?

options.why: Write is for producing records.
Create is for creating the topic.
Describe is for reading metadata.

questions.explain: Changing a topic's configs needs AlterConfigs on the topic; deleting it needs Delete.

questions.q: A cluster has 12 brokers. What should `bootstrap.servers` list?

options.t: All 12 brokers, or the client can't reach partitions on the others
options.why: Clients discover the full set of brokers from the ones they bootstrap with.

options.t: Several brokers, so the client can connect if one is down

options.why: Clients bootstrap from brokers, which return cluster metadata.

options.t: Exactly one broker, in leader order
options.why: Order doesn't matter, and one broker is a single point of failure for start-up.

questions.explain: `bootstrap.servers` is used for the initial connection and to discover the full set of brokers. Order doesn't matter; listing more than one is recommended in case a server is down.

questions.q: What is `client.id` for?

options.t: It must be unique per group, like group.instance.id
options.why: That is static membership; client.id has no such rule.

options.t: It authenticates the client to the broker
options.why: Authentication uses SSL or SASL, not client.id.

options.t: A logical application name in server-side request logs
It chooses which partitions a consumer gets
options.why: Assignment is done by the group protocol.

questions.explain: `client.id` is passed with requests so the source of requests can be tracked beyond IP and port, by a logical application name in server-side logs.

questions.q: Partitions were just added to a topic. How long might a running producer take to start using them, with default settings?

options.t: Up to metadata.max.age.ms (5 minutes), unless something else triggers a refresh
Never; the producer must be restarted
options.why: Clients pick up new partitions on a metadata refresh.

options.t: Instantly; the broker pushes the change to producers
options.why: Clients refresh metadata; brokers don't push it.

options.t: Until the next segment roll on the brokers
options.why: Segment rolls are unrelated to metadata.

questions.explain: New partitions appear to clients after a metadata refresh; `metadata.max.age.ms` (default 300 000 ms) forces one even with no leadership change.

questions.q: A team wants to add a tracing header to every record a producer sends, without changing each send call. Which producer setting supports this?

options.why: A partitioner chooses partitions; it doesn't change records.
Compression doesn't add headers.
client.id only names the client in logs.

questions.explain: `interceptor.classes` lists `ProducerInterceptor`s, which see (and may change) records before they are published; there are none by default.

questions.q: A producer uses `compression.type=zstd` and the team wants a better ratio at some CPU cost. Which setting adjusts this, and what is its default?

options.why: Levels are set per codec, with codec-specific names.
No such setting exists.

options.t: batch.size, which sets the compression level
options.why: batch.size sets batch size; a bigger batch can compress better, but it's not the level.

questions.explain: Each codec has a level setting: `compression.zstd.level` (default 3), `compression.lz4.level` (default 9) and `compression.gzip.level` (default -1).

questions.q: In Kafka 4.3, how do you pass producer settings (such as `acks=all`) to `kafka-console-producer`?

options.why: --producer-property is deprecated in 4.3.
--property is the older, deprecated way to pass reader properties.
The tool takes settings as options, not environment variables.

questions.explain: The 4.3 console producer takes producer settings with `--command-property` and `--command-config`; `--producer-property` and `--producer.config` are deprecated in 4.3.

questions.q: Which console consumer options print each record's key and partition alongside its value?

options.why: These options don't exist.
No such option prints keys and partitions.
--command-property passes consumer settings, not formatter settings.

questions.explain: The console consumer's formatter takes `--formatter-property` with `print.key`, `print.partition`, `print.offset`, `print.timestamp`, `print.headers` and `print.value`.

questions.q: Which TWO producer settings directly trade a little latency for higher throughput?

options.why: client.id is a label.
This chooses the security protocol.
This enables transactions.

questions.explain: `linger.ms` waits a little to fill batches, and `batch.size` sets how large a per-partition batch may grow; batching trades a little latency for throughput.

questions.q: A team needs at-most-once delivery for a metrics feed where duplicates are worse than gaps. Which combination gives it?

options.why: acks=0 is a durability choice; at-most-once also needs the consumer to commit before processing.
Those are tools for exactly-once, not at-most-once.

options.t: No producer retries, and commit before processing
Commit after processing, with retries on
options.why: That gives at-least-once.

questions.explain: The docs: at-most-once means no producer retries and committing the offset before processing.

questions.q: A topic keyed by customer ID will need much more consumer parallelism in a year. Why choose its partition count with care up front?

options.t: Adding partitions later remaps keys, and the count can never be reduced
The partition count can only be set when the cluster is formatted
options.why: Partitions can be added later; it's the side effects that matter.

options.t: More partitions make each record larger
options.why: Partition count doesn't change record size.

options.t: The partition count fixes the number of producers
options.why: Any number of producers can write to a topic.

questions.explain: Partition count caps consumer parallelism; adding partitions later changes where keys hash (breaking per-key order across the change), and it can't be reduced.

questions.q: A service must publish each product's current price so new consumers can load every product's latest price from the start of the topic. Which topic setup fits best?

options.t: Keyed by request ID, delete policy, 7-day retention
options.why: Products not updated in 7 days would vanish, and request IDs don't group a product's prices.
Without keys nothing can be compacted; every old price is kept forever.
A timestamp key keeps every price, never just the latest per product.

questions.explain: Compaction keeps at least the latest value per key, so keying by product ID gives a reader from the start every product's latest price.
